question: A manager asks to see the intermediate steps when working out which cost lines drove a budget overspend, but not when generating names for a new staff award. Why is that difference reasonable?
options: A) Because a numerical answer is more likely to be wrong than a creative answer produced for the same team.
B) Because working through a naming task takes longer than working through a numerical one of the same size.
C) Because the overspend answer can be wrong in ways only the steps reveal, while a name is judged as it stands.
D) Because name suggestions are shorter, so the reasoning behind each of them is easier to reconstruct afterwards.
correct_answers: C) Because the overspend answer can be wrong in ways only the steps reveal, while a name is judged as it stands.
explanations: This compares how error-prone the two tasks are, when the real difference is whether an answer can be wrong in a way that inspection would expose.
Relative effort is not what decides this. Steps are asked for because they can be checked, not because the task is slow.

Correct. Analysis produces a conclusion that depends on how it was reached, so the steps are what make it checkable. A proposed name either works or does not, and there is no chain of reasoning behind it to verify.
Length is incidental. Even if reconstructing the thinking behind a name were easy, doing so would not tell the manager whether the name is any good.
